| `POST` | `/inventory/{skuId}` | Add stock; creates the SKU if it is new (one atomic upsert) | `200` JSON, `400` text | Implemented; tests green; reviewed and walked through |
| `POST` | `/inventory/{skuId}/purchase` | Deduct stock, only if enough is on hand (one atomic statement; `400` body: `Insufficient inventory for <skuId>`) | `200` JSON, `400` / `404` text | Implemented; tests green; reviewed and walked through |

Request bodies are `{"quantity": <integer ≥ 1>}`. Success bodies are
`{"skuId": "...", "quantity": <integer ≥ 0>}`. Error bodies are plain-text strings
(`text/plain`), not JSON.

## Project layout

```text
build.gradle.kts         The build: plugins, dependencies, Kotlin/Java settings
settings.gradle.kts      Project name (single-module build)
gradlew, gradle/wrapper/ Gradle wrapper; pins the Gradle version, nothing to install
compose.yaml             Local Postgres for bootRun
src/main/
  kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/
    InventoryApplication.kt   Entry point; component scan starts here
    inventory/                The inventory feature: controller, service, repository, models
      error/                  Domain exceptions and the handler that maps them to HTTP errors
  resources/
    application.yml           Spring Boot configuration
    db/migration/             Flyway SQL migrations (V1__..., V2__...)
    openapi/inventory.yaml    The OpenAPI contract (source of truth)
src/test/kotlin/com/robertwoolbright/inventory/
  inventory/                  Feature tests: repository, service, controller, contract, races,
                              negative control, multi-instance, property-based, load
  support/                    Shared test setup (Testcontainers Postgres, race helper, HTTP client)
.github/workflows/       CI: tests + load test on every push, with a readable report
.claude/                 Claude Code configuration (hooks, agents, skills) — see below
CLAUDE.md                Project memory and coding standards for Claude Code
docs/
  learning/
    notes/               Study notes: one per source file, explaining it chunk by chunk
    walkthroughs/        Logs of each /walkthrough session
    kotlin-concepts.md   Index of every Kotlin/Spring concept, linked to its notes
  ai-sessions/           Exported transcripts of every AI session on this project
scripts/                 Hook scripts (branch guard, KDoc check, session export) and the CI test report
```

**Package by feature.** Code is grouped by what it does (`inventory/`), not by technical
layer (`controller/`, `service/`, `repository/`). File names still show the layer, so the
controller → service → repository flow is easy to follow. This is a general JVM/Spring
convention, not a Kotlin rule. One Kotlin difference is worth knowing: Kotlin has no
package-private visibility. Its `internal` modifier means "visible within this Gradle
module", so package boundaries are organizational, not enforced by the compiler.

web / app"]) fulfillment(["Fulfillment
services"]) subgraph edge["Edge"] r53["Route 53"] apigw["API Gateway
+ WAF"] end subgraph vpc["VPC: private subnets, 2 availability zones"] exp["Experience layer
ECS Fargate"] cart[("Cart store
ElastiCache Redis
TTL = abandonment")] alb["Internal ALB"] inv["Inventory service
ECS Fargate
2+ tasks across 2 AZs"] invcache[("Inventory read cache
ElastiCache Redis
short TTL")] rds[("RDS PostgreSQL
Multi-AZ
CHECK quantity >= 0")] end subgraph async["Messaging"] sqs[["SQS
shipment received /
return restocked"]] dlq[["Dead-letter queue"]] end customer --> r53 --> apigw --> exp exp <-->|"cart reads / writes"| cart exp -->|"GET stock, POST purchase"| alb --> inv inv -->|"1. read: cache first"| invcache inv -->|"2. on miss, and every write:
atomic SQL"| rds inv -.->|"3. after a write:
delete the cached key"| invcache fulfillment -->|"message with shipment ID"| sqs sqs -->|"consumed by"| inv sqs -.->|"after repeated failures"| dlq ``` Supporting services, left off the diagram to keep it readable: **ECR** (container images), **GitHub Actions** (build, test, deploy to ECS), **Secrets Manager** (database credentials), **CloudWatch** and **OpenTelemetry / X-Ray** (logs, metrics, traces, alarms). ## The main flows **Browsing a product page.** The experience layer asks the inventory service for a SKU. The inventory service checks its Redis cache, and on a miss reads Postgres and fills the cache with a short TTL. A slightly stale count only affects what the page displays. **Adding to cart.** The cart lives in the experience layer's Redis with a TTL, so abandoned carts expire on their own. Adding to a cart does not touch inventory; nothing is reserved. **Checkout.** The experience layer calls `POST /inventory/{skuId}/purchase`. The inventory service runs one atomic `UPDATE ... WHERE quantity >= :q` against Postgres. That statement is both the final check and the write, so there is no separate read first, and the cache is never consulted. After a successful purchase the service deletes the SKU's cache key; the next read refills it. **Receiving stock.** Fulfillment publishes a "shipment received" message with a unique shipment ID to SQS and moves on. The inventory service consumes it and calls the same service code as `POST /inventory/{skuId}`, so the same rules apply. If the inventory service is down, messages wait in the queue. Messages that keep failing go to a dead-letter queue and raise an alarm. **Returns.** `quantity` means units on hand and available to ship. Garments out on rental are not counted. A return is restocked like a shipment: once it is inspected and cleaned, fulfillment sends a message and the count goes up. ## Decisions and trade-offs | Decision | Why | Rejected alternative | | --- | --- | --- | | ECS Fargate | One Spring Boot process per container, the same as locally; no servers or cluster to manage | **EKS**: a whole cluster for one service. **Lambda**: JVM cold starts, and a DB connection per invocation (needs RDS Proxy) | | 2+ tasks across 2 AZs | Survives losing a task or a zone. Safe because the oversell guarantee lives in Postgres, not in app memory (`MultiInstanceRaceTest`) | One task: a single point of failure | | Inventory service is private | Only the experience layer can reach it, through an internal ALB | Exposing it through API Gateway: more attack surface, and clients would bypass the experience layer | | Fulfillment goes through the inventory service | The service owns its data, so its rules (atomic update, overflow guard, cache invalidation) always run | Fulfillment writing to the tables directly: skips the rules, couples to the schema, leaves the cache stale | | SQS between fulfillment and inventory | Fulfillment doesn't depend on inventory being up; messages wait and retry | Direct HTTP calls: fulfillment has to retry on its own when inventory is down | | Deduplicate by shipment ID | SQS can deliver a message more than once, and receiving *adds* stock, so a duplicate would double-count | Trusting exactly-once delivery: SQS standard queues don't promise it | | Cache-aside, delete on write, short TTL | Two writers can update Postgres and Redis in opposite orders; deleting the key can't leave a wrong value behind, and the TTL bounds any staleness | **Write-through**: the DB write and cache write aren't atomic, so the cache can end up holding an old count | | Purchases never read the cache | The atomic SQL statement is the only thing that decides whether stock is available | Checking the cache (or doing a read, then a write) at checkout: brings back the oversell race | | RDS PostgreSQL Multi-AZ | 100 TPS is a small load for one primary; Multi-AZ gives automatic failover | Aurora: worth it at larger scale; read replicas: not needed until reads strain the primary | ## What would have to change in the code - **SQS consumer:** a listener (e.g. Spring Cloud AWS `@SqsListener`) that calls `InventoryService`. - **Shipment deduplication:** a `processed_shipments` table. Insert the shipment ID and add the stock in one transaction, so a duplicate message fails on the primary key and changes nothing. - **Cache:** a Redis read path in front of `getInventory`, and key deletion after each successful write. - **Purchase idempotency:** an `Idempotency-Key` header, so a checkout retried after a timeout doesn't deduct twice. - **Operations:** Spring Actuator health checks for the ALB, credentials from Secrets Manager, and connection-pool sizing (tasks × pool size must stay under RDS `max_connections`, including during a deploy). ## When the cache earns its place At 100 TPS, Postgres serves primary-key reads in about a millisecond, and RDS bills per instance-hour, not per query. An inventory cache is worth adding when browsing traffic grows to the point where reads strain the database. The carts are a different case: they belong in Redis from day one, because they're short-lived and need to expire.

cd "C:/Users/rober/Documents/Projects/Nuuly_Inventory_Assessment" && cat >> docs/learning/interview-prep.md <<'EOF'

## Architecture and production

The full sketch, with a diagram, is in [docs/architecture.md](../architecture.md).

### How would you host this on AWS?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Route 53 and API Gateway (with WAF) in front of an experience layer, which calls the inventory service privately
through an internal ALB. Both run on ECS Fargate, the inventory service as 2+ tasks across 2 availability zones,
backed by RDS PostgreSQL Multi-AZ. Fargate because at ~100 TPS a cluster (EKS) is overkill, and Lambda means JVM
cold starts plus a database connection per invocation. Running several tasks is safe because the oversell
guarantee lives in Postgres, not in app memory: `MultiInstanceRaceTest` proves it.
</details>

### Fulfillment receives 500 units. How does that reach your database, and what if inventory is down?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Never by writing to the tables directly: the inventory service owns its data, so its rules always run.
Fulfillment publishes a "shipment received" message with a shipment ID to SQS. The inventory service consumes it
and runs the same code as `POST /inventory/{skuId}`. If inventory is down, the messages wait in the queue.

The shipment ID matters because receiving *adds* stock, and SQS can deliver a message twice. Inserting the ID into
a `processed_shipments` table in the same transaction as the stock change makes a duplicate a no-op.
</details>

### Would you put a Redis cache in front of the inventory?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

Carts, yes: they're short-lived and a TTL handles abandonment. Inventory counts only when read traffic strains
Postgres. At ~100 TPS a primary-key read is about a millisecond, and RDS bills per instance, not per query, so
a cache would add cost.

If I add one: cache-aside, delete the key on every write, short TTL. Not write-through, because the database write
and the cache write aren't atomic: two purchases can update them in opposite orders and leave an old count cached.
And a purchase never reads the cache: the atomic `UPDATE ... WHERE quantity >= :q` is the final check *and* the
write. Checking first and then writing brings back the oversell race.
</details>

### Nuuly rents clothes. What does `quantity` mean for a garment that's out with a customer?

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

`quantity` is units on hand and available to ship. Rented garments aren't counted. A return is restocked
through the same receive path once it's inspected and cleaned. With more time, I'd track individual garments with
a status (available, rented, cleaning) instead of a count.
</details>
EOF

-**Browsing a product page.** The experience layer asks the inventory service for a SKU. The inventory service
-checks its Redis cache, and on a miss reads Postgres and fills the cache with a short TTL. A slightly stale count
-only affects what the page displays.
-**Adding to cart.** The cart lives in the experience layer's Redis with a TTL, so abandoned carts expire on their
-own. Adding to a cart does not touch inventory; nothing is reserved.
-**Checkout.** The experience layer calls `POST /inventory/{skuId}/purchase`. The inventory service runs one atomic
-`UPDATE ... WHERE quantity >= :q` against Postgres. That statement is both the final check and the write, so
-there is no separate read first, and the cache is never consulted. After a successful purchase the service
-deletes the SKU's cache key; the next read refills it.
-**Receiving stock.** Fulfillment publishes a "shipment received" message with a unique shipment ID to SQS and
-moves on. The inventory service consumes it and calls the same service code as `POST /inventory/{skuId}`, so the
-same rules apply. If the inventory service is down, messages wait in the queue. Messages that keep failing go to
-a dead-letter queue and raise an alarm.

-return is restocked like a shipment: once it is inspected and cleaned, fulfillment sends a message and the count
-goes up.

-| Decision | Why | Rejected alternative |

-| ECS Fargate | One Spring Boot process per container, the same as locally; no servers or cluster to manage | **EKS**: a whole cluster for one service. **Lambda**: JVM cold starts, and a DB connection per invocation (needs RDS Proxy) |
-| 2+ tasks across 2 AZs | Survives losing a task or a zone. Safe because the oversell guarantee lives in Postgres, not in app memory (`MultiInstanceRaceTest`) | One task: a single point of failure |

-| Inventory service is private | Only the experience layer can reach it, through an internal ALB | Exposing it through API Gateway: more attack surface, and clients would bypass the experience layer |

-| Fulfillment goes through the inventory service | The service owns its data, so its rules (atomic update, overflow guard, cache invalidation) always run | Fulfillment writing to the tables directly: skips the rules, couples to the schema, leaves the cache stale |
-| SQS between fulfillment and inventory | Fulfillment doesn't depend on inventory being up; messages wait and retry | Direct HTTP calls: fulfillment has to retry on its own when inventory is down |

-| Deduplicate by shipment ID | SQS can deliver a message more than once, and receiving *adds* stock, so a duplicate would double-count | Trusting exactly-once delivery: SQS standard queues don't promise it |

-| Cache-aside, delete on write, short TTL | Two writers can update Postgres and Redis in opposite orders; deleting the key can't leave a wrong value behind, and the TTL bounds any staleness | **Write-through**: the DB write and cache write aren't atomic, so the cache can end up holding an old count |

-| Purchases never read the cache | The atomic SQL statement is the only thing that decides whether stock is available | Checking the cache (or doing a read, then a write) at checkout: brings back the oversell race |
-| RDS PostgreSQL Multi-AZ | 100 TPS is a small load for one primary; Multi-AZ gives automatic failover | Aurora: worth it at larger scale; read replicas: not needed until reads strain the primary |

-query. An inventory cache is worth adding when browsing traffic grows to the point where reads strain the database.

- **Layout:**
  - **Left to right:** Customer → Edge (Route 53 → API Gateway + WAF) → VPC.
  - **Inside the VPC:** the experience layer with its cart store, then the internal ALB → inventory service. The inventory service's numbered arrows go to the read cache and Postgres.

- **One change:** I removed the "consumed by" label on the SQS → inventory arrow because it overlapped the VPC title. The arrow already shows the direction.

-- [x] **Same-SKU purchase race.** Seed stock S, fire N > S concurrent purchases of 1 through
-      a start gate (`CountDownLatch` or coroutines) so they really overlap. Assert: exactly S

-Supporting services, left off the diagram to keep it readable: **ECR** (container images), **GitHub Actions**
-(build, test, deploy to ECS), **Secrets Manager** (database credentials), **CloudWatch** and **OpenTelemetry /
-X-Ray** (logs, metrics, traces, alarms).
-## The main flows
-**Browsing a product page.** The experience layer asks the inventory service for a SKU. The inventory service
-checks its Redis cache, and on a miss reads Postgres and fills the cache with a short TTL. A slightly stale count
-only affects what the page displays.
-**Adding to cart.** The cart lives in the experience layer's Redis with a TTL, so abandoned carts expire on their
-own. Adding to a cart does not touch inventory; nothing is reserved.
-**Checkout.** The experience layer calls `POST /inventory/{skuId}/purchase`. The inventory service runs one atomic
-`UPDATE ... WHERE quantity >= :q` against Postgres. That statement is both the final check and the write, so
-there is no separate read first, and the cache is never consulted. After a successful purchase the service
-deletes the SKU's cache key; the next read refills it.
-**Receiving stock.** Fulfillment publishes a "shipment received" message with a unique shipment ID to SQS and
-moves on. The inventory service consumes it and calls the same service code as `POST /inventory/{skuId}`, so the
-same rules apply. If the inventory service is down, messages wait in the queue. Messages that keep failing go to
-a dead-letter queue and raise an alarm.
-**Returns.** `quantity` means units on hand and available to ship. Garments out on rental are not counted. A
-return is restocked like a shipment: once it is inspected and cleaned, fulfillment sends a message and the count
-goes up.
-## Decisions and trade-offs
-| Decision | Why | Rejected alternative |

-| ECS Fargate | One Spring Boot process per container, the same as locally; no servers or cluster to manage | **EKS**: a whole cluster for one service. **Lambda**: JVM cold starts, and a DB connection per invocation (needs RDS Proxy) |
-| 2+ tasks across 2 AZs | Survives losing a task or a zone. Safe because the oversell guarantee lives in Postgres, not in app memory (`MultiInstanceRaceTest`) | One task: a single point of failure |

-| Inventory service is private | Only the experience layer can reach it, through an internal ALB | Exposing it through API Gateway: more attack surface, and clients would bypass the experience layer |

-| Fulfillment goes through the inventory service | The service owns its data, so its rules (atomic update, overflow guard, cache invalidation) always run | Fulfillment writing to the tables directly: skips the rules, couples to the schema, leaves the cache stale |
-| SQS between fulfillment and inventory | Fulfillment doesn't depend on inventory being up; messages wait and retry | Direct HTTP calls: fulfillment has to retry on its own when inventory is down |

# /ship 

Running `/ship` is Robert's go-ahead to commit, push and merge the current branch.
Report each step as you go. If any step fails, stop and explain; don't improvise
around it (no force-push, no `--no-verify`, no merging from the command line).

## 1. Pre-flight

- Current branch: `git branch --show-current`. If it's `main`, stop. There's nothing to ship,
  and work should never happen on main.
- Show `git status --short` and `git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD`.
- If there are uncommitted changes, check the file list for anything that shouldn't be
  committed (`.env`, credentials, keys, build output, IDE files, large binaries). If
  something looks wrong, stop and ask. Otherwise stage everything and commit with a concise
  message describing the change, ending with the attribution line from the system reminder.
- If there are no commits ahead of `origin/main`, stop. There's nothing to ship.

## 2. Local checks

- `python scripts/check_notes.py` must print nothing (study notes in sync). If it reports
  anything, stop and run `/sync-docs` first.
- The build and tests run in CI (step 5), not here.

## 3. Sync with main

- `git fetch origin`
- If `origin/main` has commits this branch lacks, `git merge origin/main` (a merge, not a
  rebase, so history is preserved). On conflicts, stop and walk Robert through them.

## 4. Push and open the pull request

- `git push -u origin <branch>`
- If a PR for this branch already exists (`gh pr view --json url`), reuse it.
  Otherwise, `gh pr create --base main --head <branch>` with:
  - **Title:** `` if given, otherwise a short summary of the branch's commits.
  - **Body:** a `## Summary` of what changed and why (bullets), a `## Commits` list, and the
    PR attribution line from the system reminder at the end.

## 5. Wait for CI

The `Tests` workflow (`.github/workflows/tests.yml`) runs two checks on the pull request:
**Tests** (`./gradlew build`) and **Load test** (`./gradlew loadTest`).

- `gh pr checks <number> --watch --fail-fast` waits until they finish (a few minutes).
- If any check fails, **stop; don't merge.** Give Robert the run's URL (its summary page has the
  test report with every failure and its message), explain the failure, and fix it on the branch.
  Then push again and repeat this step.
- Only continue when every check passed.

## 6. Merge

- `gh pr merge <number> --merge --delete-branch`
  - Always use `--merge`. **Never `--squash` or `--rebase`**, because the assessment reviewers
    want the full commit history. (A PreToolUse hook blocks squash and rebase.)
- `git switch main && git pull --ff-only`
- Delete the local branch if `gh` didn't: `git branch -d <branch>`.

## 7. Report

Give the PR URL, the merge commit SHA, the CI run URL, and the commits that were shipped. Remind Robert
that the next piece of work needs a new branch; the branch guard will enforce this.

-## Oversell protection: test plan
-**Invariant: a purchase must never oversell, even when requests arrive at the same moment.**
-Stock never goes below zero, and every unit sold was actually in stock. Test this at every
-level we build, using several different mechanisms, because each one catches a different
-class of bug. Each item below is also a teaching topic for a walkthrough.
-### Correctness in isolation
-- [x] Repository tests against a real Postgres (Testcontainers, not H2): purchase exact stock → 0,
-      purchase stock + 1 → rejected and quantity unchanged, purchase on missing SKU → not found
-      (`removeStock` tests, green 2026-09-29)
-- [x] Controller tests (`MockMvc`): 400 with `text/plain` body on insufficient stock, 404 on missing SKU (green 2026-09-29)
-### Concurrency
-- [x] **Same-SKU purchase race.** Seed stock S, fire N > S concurrent purchases of 1 through
-      a start gate (`CountDownLatch` or coroutines) so they really overlap. Assert: exactly S
-      succeed (200), N − S are rejected (400), final quantity is 0, never negative.
-      (`InventoryConcurrencyTest`, at the repository level; green 2026-09-29)
-- [x] **Uneven quantities.** Concurrent purchases of different sizes. Assert: the sum of
-      successful purchases ≤ S, and final = S − sum(successful). (green 2026-09-29)
-- [x] **Mixed receive + purchase race.** Concurrent restocks and purchases. Assert:
-      final = initial + sum(received) − sum(successful purchases). (green 2026-09-29)
-- [x] **New-SKU creation race.** Concurrent first-time `POST`s for a SKU that doesn't exist yet.
-      All succeed, no duplicate-key errors, final = sum of all quantities.
-      (`InventoryConcurrencyTest`, plus a lost-update race on an existing SKU; green with `addStock`, 2026-09-28)
-- [x] **Repeat to flush out flakiness.** Run the race tests many times (`@RepeatedTest`), since
-      concurrency bugs are intermittent. (all five races use `@RepeatedTest(5)`, 2026-09-29; raise the count
-      or add a stress profile if "many times" should mean more. Decided 2026-09-30: keep 5 in the normal build;
-      the `loadTest` task supplies the volume)
-- [x] **Negative control.** Show that the race check fails on a naive read-then-write purchase,
-      proving the test can actually detect an oversell. Done 2026-09-30: a permanent, test-only
-      `NaiveInventoryRepository` (Robert) runs through the shared `race()` and `assertNoOversell`;
-      a `CyclicBarrier` forces the lost update on every run (`NegativeControlTest`).
-### Database backstop
-- [x] Test that the `CHECK (quantity >= 0)` constraint rejects a direct update that would go
-      negative, so the database protects the data even if the application has a bug.
-      (`database rejects an update that would make quantity negative` in `InventoryRepositoryTest`; green since V1)
-### Across instances and under load
-- [x] **Multiple app instances.** Two app instances (or two Spring contexts) against the same
-      Postgres, running the purchase race. Correctness must hold because the database enforces it.
-      (`MultiInstanceRaceTest`: two `SpringApplicationBuilder` apps on random ports, one Testcontainers Postgres,
-      buyers split over real HTTP via `support/InventoryHttpClient`; purchase race + cross-instance restock/purchase
-      balance, `@RepeatedTest(3)`, green 2026-09-30)
-- [x] **HTTP load test.** Gatling (it has a Kotlin DSL) or k6 against the running app: sustained
-      concurrent purchases on hot SKUs, then check the final quantities with `GET /inventory`.
-      (Chosen instead: JUnit + JDK `HttpClient` on virtual threads, `InventoryLoadTest` tagged `load`, run by
-      `./gradlew loadTest`, excluded from `./gradlew test`; 50 clients x 20 s on 3 hot SKUs, exact per-SKU balance,
-      prints throughput and p50/p95/p99. 5 s run: ~2,400 req/s, green 2026-09-30)
-### Model-based (stretch)
-- [x] Property-based test (e.g. Kotest property testing): random sequences of receive and
-      purchase operations checked against a simple in-memory model. The invariant must hold
-      after every sequence. (`InventoryPropertyTest`, Kotest property 6.2.5, 200 sequences of up to 30
-      operations, compared after every step; a deliberately broken model was caught and shrunk to 2 steps, 2026-09-30)

-a dead-letter queue and raise an alarm.
-**Returns.** `quantity` means units on hand and available to ship. Garments out on rental are not counted. A
-return is restocked like a shipment: once it is inspected and cleaned, fulfillment sends a message and the count
-goes up.

-| ECS Fargate | One Spring Boot process per container, the same as locally; no servers or cluster to manage | **EKS**: a whole cluster for one service. **Lambda**: JVM cold starts, and a DB connection per invocation (needs RDS Proxy) |
-| 2+ tasks across 2 AZs | Survives losing a task or a zone. Safe because the oversell guarantee lives in Postgres, not in app memory (`MultiInstanceRaceTest`) | One task: a single point of failure |

-| Inventory service is private | Only the experience layer can reach it, through an internal ALB | Exposing it through API Gateway: more attack surface, and clients would bypass the experience layer |

-| Fulfillment goes through the inventory service | The service owns its data, so its rules (atomic update, overflow guard, cache invalidation) always run | Fulfillment writing to the tables directly: skips the rules, couples to the schema, leaves the cache stale |
-| SQS between fulfillment and inventory | Fulfillment doesn't depend on inventory being up; messages wait and retry | Direct HTTP calls: fulfillment has to retry on its own when inventory is down |
